title: Replacement of the Avionics Core Processing Standard Before the 2029 Support Cut-Off
abstract: Operator request to bring the avionics core processing standard forward on eleven aircraft before the supplier support cut-off, so that the fleet does not split into two configurations at the next cabin retrofit.

sections.request: We have been told by our avionics shop that the processing modules fitted to eleven of our aircraft go out of supplier support at the end of 2029 and that spares after that date will be repair-by-exchange only, at a price we cannot plan around. We would like Aeralis to give us a route to the current standard that we can embody during the cabin retrofit we already have booked from spring 2028, rather than as a separate visit. What matters to us is that after the work all eleven aircraft look the same to our line engineers, that the maintenance laptop still talks to them with the tooling we have, and that we do not have to retrain the crews. We are not asking for new functions. We would rather have the same aeroplane with parts we can still buy.
sections.background: Six of the eleven aircraft already carry the intermediate standard from a bulletin we embodied in 2023 and the other five are as delivered. Our shop reports four module removals in the last two years, all confirmed as no-fault-found on the bench, which we suspect is a symptom of the rack rather than the modules. The intermediate standard was sold to us as the last step before the current one, and we would like to understand whether embodying it a second time is wasted money.
sections.expected_outcome: One configuration across the eleven aircraft, supported past 2035, embodied inside the cabin retrofit slot with no additional ground time and no change to the flight crew documentation. A clear statement of what the six already-modified aircraft need, as distinct from the five that are as delivered.

type_data.business_justification: Repair-by-exchange pricing after the support cut-off is not budgetable and a split fleet configuration doubles the line engineering effort for a system the operator never touches in service.
